newsitem.title: INDIA: India's political squabbles hit tough decisions.
newsitem.headline: India's political squabbles hit tough decisions.

text.p: India's coalition partners have sunk differences to ensure political stability and a consensus on economic reforms, but squabbling has forced some tough decisions onto the backburner, analysts said on Sunday.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party split on Saturday, but breakaway leader Laloo Prasad Yadav immediately assured continued support to the ruling 15-party United Front alliance, which runs a minority government.

Two months ago, the United Front got a second lease of life after it agreed to change its leader in order to win back vital support from the Congress party. Their common foe is the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Gujral, a former communist, assured that economic liberalisation, started by the Congress party in 1991, would continue. His predecessor in the United Front, H.D. Deve Gowda, had himself initiated bold economic reforms.
"They had not (earlier) learnt the tricks of coalition. But they are learning now," political analyst Ashis Nandy of the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, told Reuters.

Analysts say India has moved into an era of Italian-style coalition politics, with the rise of aggressive regional parties and low caste groups and the eclipse of the Nehru-Gandhi political dynasty since 1991, when former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was killed by a female suicide bomber.
But they add that political stability is not a big issue.
"There is stability despite change. It will not be obvious to the people," Nandy said.
"If you see it as a long-term trend, the emerging picture is one of great stability as far as policies go," he said. "In private even CPM endorses globalisation," he said.
He was referring to the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), an alliance partner traditionally opposed to free-market policies.

But political commentator Kewal Varma said tough decisions had not been taken because of quibbling among political partners who otherwise provided a measure of political stability and endorsed a broad economic consensus on free-market policies.
"If you can't implement anything, what is the idea of policies?," Varma said. "You need an effective state even to promote a market."

Varma said the government, under pressure from communist allies, was still dragging its feet on pushing a hike in petroleum prices to lower a staggering 155-billion rupee ($4.3 billion) deficit owed to state-run oil companies arising out of subsidised fuel prices.
Communist allies say an oil price hike would hit the poor.
Similarly, political differences had stalled changes in India's patent law, Varma said. "All these policies will become counter-productive if macroeconomic stability is in danger."

Varma said Gujral's position, though secure, could be weakenend because he represented a group of less than 30 deputies in the 545-member Lok Sabha, the lower house of parliament, after 18 of its 45 members joined a breakaway group.
"The moral authority will be further weakened," Varma said. "The problem is not technical but moral."
The United Front has 178 lawmakers, and the supporting Congress party 140 in the lower house, where the two joined hands to keep out the Hindu BJP, which controls 194 votes.

Laloo Yadav broke away on Saturday with his supporters, after he alleged that voter lists in the party's presidential poll on Thursday were rigged for his rival, Sharad Yadav. Sharad Yadav, no relative of Laloo, was declared elected on Sunday.
